lesson.title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio: How Far Above the Hiss
lesson.summary: Signal-to-noise ratio expresses, in decibels, how much larger a wanted signal is than the noise floor sitting underneath it, and it is the single most common way of describing how clean a signal is.
lesson.body:
Once you have a signal and a noise floor, the natural next question is how far apart they are. Signal-to-noise ratio, universally abbreviated SNR, answers that question directly: it compares the level of a wanted signal to the level of the noise floor it rides on top of, expressed in decibels. A high SNR means the signal is comfortably above the noise and will sound clean; a low SNR means the signal and the noise are close in level, and the noise will be audible right along with, or even instead of, the signal.

The formula follows the same voltage ratio pattern used throughout this sequence: SNR (dB) = 20 times log10(V signal divided by V noise). It is the identical mathematical form used for dBu, just applied here to two actual measured voltages, a signal and a noise floor, rather than to a fixed reference.

Here is a clean worked example. Suppose a signal measures 2 V RMS, and the noise floor underneath it measures 2 mV RMS, that is, 0.002 V. The ratio is 2 divided by 0.002, which equals exactly 1000. The base ten log of 1000 is exactly 3, since 10 cubed is 1000. Multiplying by 20 gives exactly 60. So this system has an SNR of 60 dB.

There is an elegant shortcut hiding in the dBu chapter's fixed reference: because both a signal level and a noise floor can be expressed in dBu using the same 0.775 V reference, you can find SNR by simply subtracting the two dBu figures, with no need to convert back to volts at all. Take the nominal professional line level of +4 dBu, which is 1.228 V RMS, and the resistor's thermal noise floor from the last chapter, about negative 112.7 dBu. Subtracting gives 4.0 minus negative 112.7, which equals 116.7 dB. Checking this directly against the voltages confirms it: 1.228 V divided by 1.79 times 10 to the negative 6 V is about 686,034, and 20 times log10 of that comes out to about 116.7 dB as well, matching the subtraction. That agreement is not a coincidence, it works precisely because both dBu figures share the same fixed reference voltage, so subtracting them cancels the reference out and leaves the dB ratio between the two signals directly.

As a sense of scale, well designed professional audio electronics often achieve signal-to-noise ratios well above 90 to 100 dB, while a noisy, poorly shielded, or cheaply built circuit might only manage 60 or 70 dB, an audible difference on quiet passages. The next chapter builds on SNR to describe not just one signal's cleanliness, but the full span of levels a system can handle at once.
